book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

chapters.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?

Mirko Garasic reads Victor as the Modern Prometheus of the myth Plato tells in the Protagoras: like the Titan punished for stealing fire, Victor's purely technical gift of life fails because, as Zeus tells Hermes, justice and reverence must be shared by all or cities cannot exist. The chapter's real subject is love - Prometheus suffers for loving the humans he made, and the creature asks for a female companion while Victor's hate-filled destruction of her unleashes the second wave of revenge. Tim Burton's Frankenweenie splits this love/hate dualism: young Victor's tear over Sparky makes the experiment work, the classmates' prize-greed and the xenophobic mayor produce the real monsters, and Mr. Rzykruski teaches that science severed from emotion is empty. Via Zygmunt Bauman's liquid modernity, Garasic concludes that our own detached, networked isolation is the danger: scientific progress alone never makes a better society, love and community do.

Spyros Petrounakos reads Frankenstein as a Cartesian narrative whose external events run parallel to the inner worlds of Victor and the creature, from Victor's solitary conception of 'bestowing animation upon lifeless matter' to his imprisonment in a truth nobody would believe when Justine's life is at stake. The monster's acquisition of language at the De Lacey cottage - grasping 'fire, milk, and bread' but not 'good,' 'dearest,' and 'unhappy' - becomes the test case between Descartes's private inner theater (with its evil demon) and Gilbert Ryle's reply, glossing Locke on ideas of reflection, that we learn emotion words by responding directly to behavior rather than by cracking a hidden code. On Ryle's reading the monster's deformity is horror precisely because it is put to Cartesian use, a body that seems to shield its inner life, so the creature only truly comes alive when it behaves like a human being.

Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.

Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.

Mike Kugler argues Shelley's novel tests the radical idealism of her father William Godwin, her mother Mary Wollstonecraft, and her husband Percy: Victor's Promethean project of perfecting humanity in isolation, away from the 'intimate circle' of family and friends, produces a creature whose natural benevolence is destroyed only by repeated exclusion, first by the De Laceys. Drawing on Rousseau's and Wollstonecraft's view that children raised by benevolent parents develop their innate sympathy, the chapter reads the creature as an abandoned child - a new Adam who becomes a Satanic rebel when every community rejects him - and Victor's attempt at reproduction without women and mothers as the novel's deepest violation. The redemptive counterfactual is adoption: what if Victor had raised the creature in his home, as his father did Elizabeth?

Jeff Ewing reads Victor's science through ecofeminist and Marxist critiques: M. Waldman's promise to 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' and 'show how she works in her hiding-places' exemplifies exactly what Val Plumwood condemns - male knowers wringing secrets from a nature pictured as a passive female slave - and Victor studies natural elements 'in their death, not in their life' as raw material for power. Marx and Engels supply the parallel diagnosis: capitalism biases science and technology toward profit, turning tools and knowledge into means of domination rather than human flourishing, just as Victor's knowledge serves only his glory and kills everyone he loves. The chapter concludes that we breed Frankenstein's monsters whenever science treats nature, workers, women, and othered peoples as mere instruments, and only replacing those social relations frees science from power and profit.

Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.

Jessie Dern uses Derrida's Rogues and The Animal that Therefore I Am to show that naming is power: Victor cries 'Devil!' before the creature has done anything, and labels like 'monster,' 'rogue,' and 'animal' are performative verdicts that reveal the labeler, who secures his own goodness by negating the Other, more than the labeled. The novel multiplies the pattern, from Justine's confessor making her 'think that I was the monster that he said I was' to Elizabeth's 'men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other's blood,' while Victor, guarding his self-image, becomes the monster himself. Against the Nietzsche epigraph about fighting monsters, the chapter closes with Derrida's playful self-application ('the animal that therefore I am') as the move the creature never gets to make: contesting the label and claiming a name and a self.

John Karavitis uses Dean Koontz's series, in which Victor Helios/Frankenstein engineers a 'New Race' lacking free will and empathy, to test the bioethics of human enhancement: Michael Sandel's bioconservative Case against Perfection condemns enhancements that bypass effort and agency - performance-enhancing drugs, off-label Ritalin and growth hormone, designer children - as a 'Promethean aspiration to remake nature' that destroys human nature. Allen Buchanan's bioprogressive reply that evolution's blind tinkering can be safely improved upon is challenged by the bonobo/chimpanzee contrast, dogs versus wolves, and Belyaev's tame silver foxes, all showing that small genetic changes cascade into large behavioral and physical ones. Since behavior defines morality, the chapter concludes that genetically remaking ourselves risks remaking morality itself, ending in Koontz's posthuman world where 'efficiency equaled morality' and inefficiency was the only sin.

Joe Slater builds a two-premise anti-natalist argument from Shelley's Paradise Lost epigraph ('Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man?'): since it is wrong to inflict harm on an autonomous being without consent, and every autonomous life inevitably contains harms, creating autonomous beings - Adam in the lab or a baby in the womb - is wrong. He answers the objection from Parfit's non-identity problem via the damaged-brain Adam case, and defends the Harm Premise with Mill's On Liberty: consent matters because autonomous agents must be free to harm themselves, as with the smoker, the drinker, and Frankenstein's stolen kidney. G.E. Moore's 'Moorean shift' and Benatar's genetic, social, and institutional pro-natal biases explain why we resist the conclusion, with a 'Super Adam' incapable of harm as the only escape.

Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.

William Rodriguez argues Branagh's 1994 Mary Shelley's Frankenstein deliberately overturns what Plato's account of art as mimesis that forms character, and Colin McGinn's aesthetic theory of virtue (G-beings versus E-beings), lead us to expect - that beauty of soul shows in beauty of body - since the handsome Victor is the moral degenerate while De Niro's hideous creature is a moral virtuoso whose first words are 'friend' and 'father.' The beautiful Frankenstein family harbors ugliness: Oedipal scenes between Victor and his mother Caroline, the wedding that makes Elizabeth 'brother, sister no more; husband and wife,' and Victor's relish in abandoning his creation. The creature's questions - 'Do I have a soul?', 'Who am I?' - and his secret harvest for the peasant family credit moral worth to the ugly, so the monster fascinates us because the monster is us: evil may be attractive and lurking inside rather than deformed and outside.

holes.name: Zygmunt Bauman
holes.what: Sociologist-philosopher of 'liquid modernity,' the light, individualized late modernity in which communal bonds dissolve and the foreigner or Other appears as a threat.
holes.why: Chapter 28 frames Victor's self-imposed isolation and our own networked detachment through Bauman's liquid modernity, and no existing slug covers him or it.

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of the cyborg, the hybrid of organism and machine that dissolves nature/culture and self/other boundaries and is 'exceedingly unfaithful' to its patriarchal origins.
holes.why: Chapter 30 devotes a section to reading Frankenstein's creature as Haraway's cyborg - an illegitimate offspring rebelling against the father - to undermine Western self/other ideology.

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that humanity should be understood, and may be remade, beyond traditional humanism, rejecting fixed natural/artificial and human/other boundaries (Pepperell's distinction between momentary consciousness and accumulated being).
holes.why: Chapter 30's central claim is that we may be ready to move beyond humanism and accept a 'new Frankenstein,' and the taxonomy has no posthumanist or transhumanist slug.

holes.name: William Godwin
holes.what: Radical British philosopher of political justice and human perfectibility, Mary Shelley's father, notorious for his attacks on marriage and the diminishment of family bonds.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Frankenstein as Shelley's response to Godwin's utopian individualism, whose dreams of the perfectible man Victor embodies and the creature's fate tests.

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's account of the frightening that emerges from the familiar and repressed (via Schelling: what ought to have remained hidden but has come to light), felt before whatever blurs living and dead, self and other.
holes.why: Chapter 35's middle section explains the creature's horror - human enough to resemble us, deformed enough to repel - through the uncanny, which no existing slug names.

holes.name: Allen E. Buchanan
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends biomedical enhancement, arguing in Better than Human that evolution's haphazard course can be safely and beneficially improved upon.
holes.why: Chapter 38 stages the enhancement debate as Sandel's bioconservatism against Buchanan's bioprogressivism, and the taxonomy covers only the former.

holes.name: David Benatar
holes.what: Philosopher of anti-natalism who argues in Better Never to Have Been that coming into existence is always a serious harm.
holes.why: Chapter 39's argument that creating monsters or babies is wrong is explicitly informed by Benatar's book, including his diagnosis of pro-natal bias.

holes.name: Anti-Natalism
holes.what: The view that it is wrong to bring new autonomous (or sentient) beings into existence, whether by procreation or by creation.
holes.why: Chapter 39 is built around defining and defending anti-natalism, applying it equally to conceiving children and to Frankenstein's act of creation.

holes.name: The Non-Identity Problem
holes.what: Parfit's puzzle that choices determining who will exist seem to wrong no existing, or even identical, future person, complicating duties to future people.
holes.why: Chapter 39 must answer it - via the case of Frankenstein activating a damaged brain rather than building a healthy one - for its claim that creating life wrongs the created.

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: Enlightenment satirist-philosopher who, after the Lisbon earthquake, rejected optimistic theodicy (Candide) and held that morality demands we not pretend to make evil intelligible.
holes.why: Chapter 40 frames the monster's problem of evil through the Rousseau-Voltaire rivalry and Candide's 'tend to our garden,' yet Voltaire is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Susan Neiman
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who reads modernity itself as born from the Lisbon earthquake's destruction of theodicy, in the clash between Rousseau's and Voltaire's responses to evil.
holes.why: Chapter 40 explicitly adopts Neiman's account of the problem of evil as its central frame for reading the monster as a modern Job.

holes.name: Colin McGinn
holes.what: Philosopher whose Ethics, Evil and Fiction connects moral evaluation to aesthetics, holding that virtue is beauty of soul and vice its ugliness (the aesthetic theory of virtue, G-beings and E-beings).
holes.why: Chapter 41's reading of Branagh's film as inverting our beauty-based moral judgments is built throughout on McGinn's aesthetic theory of virtue.
